what_its_for: Ibrutinib is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of blood cancers, including chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), Waldenström's macroglobulinemia, marginal zone lymphoma, and chronic graft-versus-host disease. It works by blocking a protein that helps cancer cells grow and survive, which helps slow or stop the cancer from spreading.
how_to_take: Swallow ibrutinib capsules or tablets whole with a full glass of water. Do not open, break, or chew the capsules or tablets. You may take it with or without food, but try to take it at the same time every day. If you are taking tablets, you can split them if needed, but do not crush or chew them. Wash your hands after handling the tablets or capsules.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition and other medicines you take. The usual doses range from 140 mg to 560 mg once daily, depending on what you are being treated for. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly. Do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and it is still the same day, take it as soon as you remember. If the next day has already started, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular time. Do not take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store ibrutinib at room temperature between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it in the original container with the lid tightly closed. Keep it away from heat, light, and moisture. Keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medicine down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a medicine take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, Seville oranges, and starfruit while taking ibrutinib, as they can increase the amount of medicine in your blood and raise your risk of side effects. Avoid St. John's Wort supplements, as they can make ibrutinib less effective. Avoid blood thinners like warfarin or fish oil supplements without talking to your doctor first, as ibrutinib increases your risk of bleeding. Avoid live vaccines while on this medicine. Avoid contact sports or activities that could cause injury and bleeding.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: unusual or heavy bleeding (blood in urine, stool, or vomit; prolonged nosebleeds; heavy periods), signs of infection (fever over 100.4°F, chills, cough, painful urination), chest pain, shortness of breath, or irregular heartbeat (these could be signs of a serious heart problem), sudden severe headache, vision changes, weakness, or numbness (possible signs of stroke), severe stomach pain or diarrhea, swelling in your legs or ankles, or a skin rash. Also call your doctor before any surgery or dental procedure.
when_it_works: Ibrutinib starts working right away in your body, but it may take several weeks to months before you notice improvements in your symptoms or before your doctor sees changes in your test results. It is very important to keep taking it every day even if you feel well. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and older) may be more sensitive to side effects, especially bleeding and infections, so close monitoring is important. Women who are pregnant or planning to become pregnant should not use this medicine, as it can harm an unborn baby. Both men and women should use effective birth control during treatment and for 1 to 3 months after stopping. Do not breastfeed while taking ibrutinib. If you have liver or kidney problems, your doctor may need to adjust your dose. Always tell your doctor and pharmacist about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as many drugs can interact with ibrutinib.
